origins: Debt can come from many roads: a job loss, an illness, a divorce, a family emergency, school, rising prices, or simply choices we now regret. But family and culture often attach one meaning to all of them: “You must have been careless.” If a parent was ashamed of owing money, or if people judged us for it, we may carry that verdict even when the facts are more complicated.
teaches: Scripture is honest about debt. Proverbs says the borrower is slave to the lender, and it also values careful planning. But Scripture never says that owing money defines a person. Paul writes that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. God knows our frame and is mindful that we are dust, and He has not dealt with us according to our sins. Where we did make poor choices, we can own them, learn, and move forward. Where we did not, we can let go of a verdict that was never ours to carry.
self_statements: Only careless people end up in debt.
Everyone can see I cannot manage money.
My debt shows what kind of person I am.
If I were responsible, I would not owe.
errors: Calling myself “irresponsible” instead of describing what happened.
Seeing myself as either totally responsible or a total failure with money.
Blaming myself for things that were outside my control, such as illness or layoffs.
Focusing on the debt and ignoring the ways I have been responsible.
questions: How did the debt actually happen, and which parts were choices and which were circumstances?
What have I done responsibly, such as working, caring for others, or paying on time?
Would I call a friend in my situation “irresponsible”?
Where did I learn that debt equals failure?
What does God say about my worth when I owe?
What is one wise next step I can take without condemning myself?
truth: Owing money describes my account, not my character. Some of it may come from my choices and some from things I could not control. Either way, in Christ I am not condemned. I can be honest about the past, take wise steps now, and trust God’s mercy.
hw_truths: My debt does not define me.
There is no condemnation for me in Christ.
I can be honest about what happened without attacking myself.
God knows my frame and is mindful that I am dust.
I can take one wise step at a time.
log: Each day, write one fact about your money situation and one thing you did responsibly. Notice whether the harsh label softens.
actions: List how the debt happened. Mark what was a choice, what was circumstance, and what you have learned.
Cross out “irresponsible” and write a plain description, such as “I owe $X and I am making a plan.”
Make a list of what you owe, or call one creditor, or schedule a visit with a trusted advisor or counselor.
Read Romans 8:1 each morning for a week.
prayer: Father, You know how my debt came about. Forgive what I need to be forgiven for, and free me from labels You do not give me. Help me take wise steps and rest in Your mercy. Amen.
hw_questions: Which parts were choices and which were circumstances?
What label am I using on myself?
What does God say about me?
What is one wise step this week?
name_example: Sarah can write: “There is no condemnation for me in Christ, so I can face my debt honestly and take one wise step.”
meta: Christian belief counseling for “My debt proves I'm irresponsible.” with BSB scriptures, questions, songs, and practical homework.
